341.quote_or_event: “But a man who is indifferent to ‘colours,’ is free from sorrows; though still in the Saṃsâra, he is not affected by that long succession of pains, just as the leaf of the Lotus (is not moistened) by water.”
341.explanation: Mahāvīra's sermon on the causes of carelessness goes through the senses one by one. For each object (colours, sounds, smells, tastes, touches, feelings) it shows that passion for it brings pain and indifference to it ends that pain.
341.tie_back: Valluvar's doubled 'from whatever, from that' sets up the same one-to-one ledger: each object a person becomes indifferent to stops causing that person pain.
341.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.34 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 189)
341._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The text repeats this verse, with the object changed, for each of the six sense-fields, which closely mirrors the Kural's object-by-object logic.

342.quote_or_event: “You are now a king of great power and prosperity, enjoying the reward of your good actions; put from you the transitory pleasures, and enter the order for the sake of the highest good!”
342.explanation: The monk Citra urges his former brother, now the universal monarch Brahmadatta, to renounce while he is still at the height of his wealth and power. The king cannot let go, and the lecture records the bad end that follows.
342.tie_back: The Kural says to renounce while there is still something to renounce. Citra gives exactly that advice to a man who holds everything.
342.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.20 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 59)
342._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The timing theme fits well, but the Kural's promise of many joys 'here' is not stated in this verse.

343.quote_or_event: “He should not desire (pleasant) sounds and colours, but conquer his longing for all kinds of pleasures. A monk should avoid every attachment and bear every pain, be full (of wisdom), not greedy, wander about homeless, give assurance of safety (to all beings), and be free from passions.”
343.explanation: The Sūtrakṛtāṅga tells the monk to master the pull of the sense-objects and, at the same time, to give up every attachment, living homeless and free of passion.
343.tie_back: Valluvar pairs conquering the five senses with giving up 'together' everything they crave. These verses join the same two duties: overcome the longing for sounds and colours, and avoid every attachment.
343.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.7.27-28 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 296)
343._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com (the opening 'He' is capitalised for the excerpt). The twofold structure is strongly parallel, but the verse names only sounds and colours rather than all five senses, and lacks the Kural's 'all at once' emphasis.

344.quote_or_event: “He who owns even a small property in living or lifeless things, or consents to others holding it, will not be delivered from misery.”
344.explanation: In the opening answer of the Sūtrakṛtāṅga, Sudharman gives Mahāvīra's account of what binds the soul. Possessing even a little property, or approving of others holding it, is named first.
344.tie_back: The Kural says owning even one thing drags the ascetic back into delusion. The Jain canon makes the same uncompromising claim: even a small property blocks deliverance. This is the root of the monastic vow of aparigraha.
344.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.1.1.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 235)
344._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. A near one-to-one match: both make even the smallest possession fatal to the renunciant's goal.

345.quote_or_event: “(In order to be able) to practise control a monk should eat; he should desire to get rid of sin … he should wait for the advent of death; having annihilated his Karman he should not again mix with the world, but be rather like a car whose axle is broken.”
345.explanation: The monk keeps up the body only as an instrument of self-control. Freed of karma, he never re-enters the round of worldly existence, like a cart whose axle is broken.
345.tie_back: Valluvar treats the body as surplus to someone set on ending births. The Jain text likewise allows food only so that control can be practised, and points beyond the body to a soul that never again 'mixes with the world'.
345.source: Sūtrakṛtāṅga I.7.29-30 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 296-297)
345._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com, with an ellipsis marking omitted words. The body-as-instrument idea matches Parimelazhagar's gloss, but the text does not explicitly call the body an excess or a tie.

346.quote_or_event: “He who ceasing from acts relinquishes the idea of property, relinquishes property itself. That sage has seen the path (to final liberation) for whom there exists no property.”
346.explanation: The Ācārāṅga puts the root of possession in the mind. The real renunciation is giving up the idea of 'mine', and the sage for whom nothing is 'his' has found the road to liberation.
346.tie_back: Valluvar says that cutting away the pride of 'I' and 'mine' leads to a world above the gods. The Ācārāṅga likewise makes dropping the sense of 'mine' the doorway to final liberation, which in Jain cosmology lies above every heaven.
346.source: Ācārāṅga Sūtra I.2.6.2 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 22, 1884, pp. 25-26)
346._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Jacobi's 'idea of property' renders mine-ness, which fits enadhu well. The text does not address the 'I' (ahaṅkāra) side as directly.

347.quote_or_event: “As the crane is produced from an egg, and the egg is produced from a crane, so they call desire the origin of delusion, and delusion the origin of desire.”
347.explanation: Mahāvīra describes a closed loop: desire produces delusion, and delusion produces desire again, like crane and egg. Elsewhere in the same lecture this cycle is shown to generate karma and misery.
347.tie_back: Valluvar's mirrored phrase, sorrows that seize and never let go of those who seize and never let go, enacts the same self-feeding cycle that the crane-and-egg image describes.
347.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.6 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)
347._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Both have a strong circular structure, though the Jain loop runs between desire and delusion rather than between clinging and sorrow.

348.quote_or_event: “As an elephant, sinking down in a quagmire, sees the raised ground but does not get to the shore, so do we who long for sensual pleasures, not follow the path of monks.” … “But Kitra the great sage, of excellent conduct and penance, was indifferent to pleasure; after he had practised the highest self-control, he reached the highest place of perfection.”
348.explanation: King Brahmadatta admits that he is stuck like an elephant in a swamp and cannot leave his pleasures, and he ends in hell. His brother Citra renounces fully and reaches perfection.
348.tie_back: The Kural's sharp contrast between those who renounce completely and reach the goal and those caught in the net is acted out by the two brothers. One is mired, the other reaches the summit.
348.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 13.30 and 13.35 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, pp. 60-61)
348._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The image is a quagmire rather than a net, but the binary between complete renouncer and trapped worldling is closely parallel.

349.quote_or_event: “Misery ceases on the absence of delusion, delusion ceases on the absence of desire, desire ceases on the absence of greed, greed ceases on the absence of property.”
349.explanation: The Uttarādhyayana traces misery back through delusion, desire and greed to possession. Remove the last link and the whole chain collapses.
349.tie_back: Valluvar says that births are cut at the very moment attachment ceases. The Jain chain likewise makes the end of misery depend directly on the end of grasping.
349.source: Uttarādhyayana Sūtra 32.8 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895, p. 185)
349._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The causal logic matches closely. The verse speaks of misery rather than rebirth by name, though the preceding verse (32.7) identifies birth and death as that misery.

350.quote_or_event: Samantabhadra's hymn to the twelfth Tīrthaṅkara, Vāsupūjya, says that worship serves no purpose for the Jina, who is free from attachment, and that blame means nothing to one who has cast off enmity. Yet remembering his pure qualities cleanses the devotee's mind of the stains of sin.
350.explanation: Jain devotion is directed to the vītarāga, 'one free of attachment'. Since the Jina grants nothing, the benefit of devotion comes entirely from fixing the mind on detachment itself.
350.tie_back: Valluvar tells us to cling to the One who is without attachment so that every other attachment falls away. Jain worship of the passionless Jina works by exactly this method, although the Jina is a liberated soul, not a creator God.
350.source: Svayambhūstotra of Samantabhadra, verse 57 (Vāsupūjya-stuti), Sanskrit text at sanskritdocuments.org
350._accuracy_note: The Sanskrit verse was checked on sanskritdocuments.org; the English is my own paraphrase. The 'cling to the detached one' strategy fits closely, but most commentators read patratraan as God, which Jain non-theism does not accept.
